P3L5 Collision Simulation Lab - Student Notebook

Sarah M. - Period 3

Background & Hypothesis

The relationship we’re testing: \(\frac{m_A}{m_B} = -\frac{\Delta v_B}{\Delta v_A}\)

My Hypothesis: I think this relationship will work for all types of collisions because the math seems pretty solid. But I’m not sure about the elastic vs inelastic thing - maybe when they stick together it’s different?

Variables I’m testing:

  • Independent: collision type (elastic/inelastic), mass ratios, initial velocities
  • Dependent: final velocities, velocity changes
  • Controls: using same simulation, keeping other variables constant when testing one thing

Data Collection

Trial 1: Control (repeat from previous lesson)

  • Purpose: Make sure our relationship still works
  • Setup: Cart A = 2 kg at 4 m/s, Cart B = 1 kg at 0 m/s, Elastic collision

Results:

  • Cart A final: 1.33 m/s
  • Cart B final: 5.33 m/s

Calculations:

  • $\Delta v_A = 1.33 - 4 = -2.67$ m/s
  • $\Delta v_B = 5.33 - 0 = +5.33$ m/s
  • Mass ratio: $\frac{m_A}{m_B} = \frac{2}{1} = 2$
  • Velocity ratio: $-\frac{\Delta v_B}{\Delta v_A} = -\frac{5.33}{-2.67} = 2.00$

Test: Does $2 = 2$? YES! ✓

Trial 2: Test Collision Type (Elastic → Inelastic)

  • Purpose: Same setup as Trial 1, but inelastic collision
  • Setup: Cart A = 2 kg at 4 m/s, Cart B = 1 kg at 0 m/s, Inelastic collision

Results:

  • Cart A final: 2.67 m/s
  • Cart B final: 2.67 m/s (they stick together!)

Calculations:

  • $\Delta v_A = 2.67 - 4 = -1.33$ m/s
  • $\Delta v_B = 2.67 - 0 = +2.67$ m/s
  • Mass ratio: $\frac{m_A}{m_B} = \frac{2}{1} = 2$
  • Velocity ratio: $-\frac{\Delta v_B}{\Delta v_A} = -\frac{2.67}{-1.33} = 2.01$

Test: Does $2 ≈ 2.01$? YES! ✓ (close enough - probably rounding error)

Observation: Even when they stick together, the math still works!

Trial 3: Test Mass Ratio (1:1)

  • Purpose: Try equal masses
  • Setup: Cart A = 3 kg at 5 m/s, Cart B = 3 kg at 0 m/s, Elastic collision

Results:

  • Cart A final: 0 m/s
  • Cart B final: 5 m/s

Calculations:

  • $\Delta v_A = 0 - 5 = -5$ m/s
  • $\Delta v_B = 5 - 0 = +5$ m/s
  • Mass ratio: $\frac{m_A}{m_B} = \frac{3}{3} = 1$
  • Velocity ratio: $-\frac{\Delta v_B}{\Delta v_A} = -\frac{5}{-5} = 1$

Test: Does $1 = 1$? YES! ✓

Cool observation: With equal masses, they completely exchange velocities!

Trial 4: Test Both Moving (Head-on collision)

  • Purpose: Both carts moving toward each other
  • Setup: Cart A = 2 kg at 3 m/s, Cart B = 1 kg at -2 m/s, Elastic collision

Results:

  • Cart A final: -1 m/s
  • Cart B final: 4 m/s

Calculations:

  • $\Delta v_A = -1 - 3 = -4$ m/s
  • $\Delta v_B = 4 - (-2) = +6$ m/s
  • Mass ratio: $\frac{m_A}{m_B} = \frac{2}{1} = 2$
  • Velocity ratio: $-\frac{\Delta v_B}{\Delta v_A} = -\frac{6}{-4} = 1.5$

Test: Does $2 = 1.5$? NO! ✗

Hmm… Let me check my math… recalculates… Wait, that’s still what I get. Maybe I made an error in the simulation?

Retry: Let me try this again…

  • Cart A final: -0.33 m/s
  • Cart B final: 4.67 m/s

New calculations:

  • $\Delta v_A = -0.33 - 3 = -3.33$ m/s
  • $\Delta v_B = 4.67 - (-2) = +6.67$ m/s
  • Velocity ratio: $-\frac{\Delta v_B}{\Delta v_A} = -\frac{6.67}{-3.33} = 2.00$

Test: Does $2 = 2$? YES! ✓

Note: I must have misread the simulation the first time. The math works!

Trial 5: Test Velocity Magnitude (High Speed)

  • Purpose: Same mass ratio as Trial 1, but higher speeds
  • Setup: Cart A = 2 kg at 10 m/s, Cart B = 1 kg at 0 m/s, Elastic collision

Results:

  • Cart A final: 3.33 m/s
  • Cart B final: 13.33 m/s

Calculations:

  • $\Delta v_A = 3.33 - 10 = -6.67$ m/s
  • $\Delta v_B = 13.33 - 0 = +13.33$ m/s
  • Mass ratio: $\frac{m_A}{m_B} = \frac{2}{1} = 2$
  • Velocity ratio: $-\frac{\Delta v_B}{\Delta v_A} = -\frac{13.33}{-6.67} = 2.00$

Test: Does $2 = 2$? YES! ✓

Observation: Speed doesn’t matter - the relationship still holds!

Trial 6: Extreme Mass Ratio (10:1)

  • Purpose: Test with very different masses
  • Setup: Cart A = 10 kg at 2 m/s, Cart B = 1 kg at 0 m/s, Elastic collision

Results:

  • Cart A final: 1.64 m/s
  • Cart B final: 3.64 m/s

Calculations:

  • $\Delta v_A = 1.64 - 2 = -0.36$ m/s
  • $\Delta v_B = 3.64 - 0 = +3.64$ m/s
  • Mass ratio: $\frac{m_A}{m_B} = \frac{10}{1} = 10$
  • Velocity ratio: $-\frac{\Delta v_B}{\Delta v_A} = -\frac{3.64}{-0.36} = 10.11$

Test: Does $10 ≈ 10.11$? YES! ✓ (close - probably rounding)

Observation: Heavy object barely slows down, light object speeds up a lot!

Analysis Questions

1. Hypothesis Evaluation

My hypothesis was mostly right! The relationship works for both elastic and inelastic collisions. I was surprised that it worked even when the carts stick together - I thought that might break the math somehow.

2. Variable Analysis

Biggest effect: None of the variables broke the relationship! That’s actually surprising. Least effect: The actual speeds didn’t matter at all - Trial 5 with high speeds worked just like Trial 1 with lower speeds.

3. Pattern Recognition

The mathematical relationship held for ALL my collision scenarios. Even the extreme mass ratio (10:1) worked, just with some tiny rounding errors.

4. Experimental Design

Changing one variable at a time was really helpful! Like comparing Trials 1 and 2 showed me that elastic vs inelastic doesn’t matter for the math. And comparing Trials 1 and 5 showed that speed doesn’t matter either.

5. Error Analysis

I had some small differences (like 2.01 instead of 2.00) but I think that’s just from rounding in the simulation. My mistake in Trial 4 showed me I need to be more careful reading the numbers!

6. Scientific Conclusion

Based on my testing, I think this IS a universal law of physics! It worked for:

  • Different collision types (elastic vs inelastic)
  • Different mass ratios (1:1, 2:1, 10:1)
  • Different speeds (slow and fast)
  • Different starting conditions (one moving, both moving)

The math is consistent across all these different situations, which suggests it’s a fundamental rule about how collisions work.

Reflection

This lab really surprised me! I expected the relationship to break down in some cases, but it held up every time. The coolest discovery was that it works for inelastic collisions too - I didn’t expect that.

The hardest part was being careful with the calculations, especially keeping track of positive and negative signs. But once I got into a rhythm, it became easier.

I’m convinced now that this momentum conservation thing is real and universal. It makes me wonder what other “hidden” mathematical relationships exist in physics that we just haven’t discovered yet!
